muralha.name: City Wall and Alfândega Tower (“Aqui nasceu Portugal”)
muralha.short: Guimarães' medieval wall and the only surviving tower, the Alfândega, with the inscription “Aqui nasceu Portugal”
muralha.long: Between the late 12th and early 13th century King Sancho I is said to have ridden round the upper town to mark its boundary — probably when Guimarães was first walled. Denis completed the circuit in 1318, uniting two previously independent settlements in one defence with eight gates, six towers and two corner turrets. The double wall withstood the sieges of 1322, 1369 and 1385, and João I ordered the inner wall between the two settlements demolished. In the 19th century the stone was quarried for building; only two stretches and the Alfândega tower survived — the last remaining tower. It bears the inscription “Aqui nasceu Portugal”.
muralha.history:
Between the late 12th and early 13th century King Sancho I, son of Afonso Henriques, is said to have ridden round the upper part of the town to mark its boundary; it was probably from this time that the town began to be walled. Guimarães was then made up of two independent settlements, and in the first two centuries of Portuguese nationhood it was the upper burgh — the nucleus around the castle — that was more heavily fortified, rather than the lower town, which had grown up around the collegiate church of Oliveira.

In the 13th century, on the initiative of King Afonso III, work began on the definitive line of the wall, completed in 1318 under King Dinis. Both burghs of Guimarães gained a single defensive structure, centred on the castle but reaching out to the community and the main religious institutions. Eight gates, six towers and two cubelos (corner bastions) closed a fairly long military perimeter.

In the years that followed, the double wall of Guimarães withstood three sieges: in 1322, when the Infante Afonso made war on his father Dinis; in 1369, when Castilian troops under Henry II invaded the Entre-Douro-e-Minho; and in 1385, when João I besieged the resisting Vimaranenses. It was this king who ordered the inner wall dividing the two burghs to be demolished, declaring that both should become one people.

In the 19th century, as with the castle and the Dukes' Palace, the stones of the wall were used as a quarry for public and private buildings. This destroyed almost every tower and gate by the middle of the 20th century; further destruction followed with the laying of new roads. Today two important stretches survive. The longest runs from Largo da Condessa Mumadona along the whole of Avenida Alberto Sampaio; the second, a little further south, is associated with the old Alfândega tower.

The Torre da Alfândega stands in the very heart of the city. It is the only surviving tower of the medieval wall, still almost untouched since it was built in the 13th century; it is classed as a national monument and carries the wall panel inscribed “Aqui Nasceu Portugal” — “Portugal was born here”. The tower takes its name from the customs house (alfândega) that once stood nearby. After restoration to a design by the architects Margarida Morais and Miguel Melo, it reopened to the public on 3 August 2024: free entry, from 10:00 to 18:00, and it is to become an interpretive centre.

In 2019 a pedestrian route along the wall-walk was laid out inside the longest stretch of wall — the Percurso Pedonal do Adarve da Muralha. One entrance is beside the entrance to the Alberto Sampaio Museum, and the exit is at Largo da Condessa Mumadona; entry is free, winter from 10:00 to 17:00, summer from 10:00 to 21:00.

The wall and tower are a reminder that Guimarães was a fortress on the frontier of the young kingdom: here, tradition says, Portugal was born. The inscription “Aqui Nasceu Portugal” on the Alfândega tower has become one of the city's symbols, and the ensemble itself is a national monument. The wall-walk opened in 2019 gave the townspeople access once more to the wall, with a panorama over the castle, the Dukes' Palace and Monte da Penha. The restoration of the tower in 2024 continued that work: the monument is open again, entry is free, and an interpretive centre on the history of the town's defences is planned inside.
facts: The definitive wall was begun under Afonso III and completed in 1318 under King Dinis.
It had eight gates, six towers and two corner bastions (cubelos).
The double wall withstood the sieges of 1322, 1369 and 1385.
João I ordered the inner wall between the two burghs demolished, making them one town.
The Torre da Alfândega is the only surviving tower of Guimarães' medieval wall.
The tower reopened to the public on 3 August 2024; it bears the inscription “Aqui Nasceu Portugal”.
muralha.tip: Visiting is free. The Alfândega tower is open daily from 10:00 to 18:00. The pedestrian wall-walk (Percurso do Adarve) is free: winter (23 September – 19 March) from 10:00 to 17:00, summer from 10:00 to 21:00; its entrance is beside the Alberto Sampaio Museum, with the exit at Largo da Condessa Mumadona. Start at Largo da Condessa Mumadona and walk along Avenida Alberto Sampaio: from the wall you can see the Dukes' Palace, the castle and Penha. Combine it with the Alberto Sampaio Museum and the inscribed tower by the Toural.
